These sample-only priors cannot be used directly in likelihood-based normalizing flows, which require evaluating the prior density. We propose Projected Characteristic-Function matching (PCF), a density-free framework for learning an invertible map between a data distribution and a prior specified only through samples.
  Our method aligns distributions using projected empirical characteristic functions, eliminating the need for density estimation, adversarial training, or paired observations. To address the non-uniqueness of the transport map, we introduce an optional transport regularizer that selects lower-displacement transformations while preserving endpoint alignment.
  We benchmark PCF on controlled transports, sample-efficiency studies, and high-dimensional alignment tasks. PCF matches the accuracy of kernel MMD on the controlled benchmark and on raw-pixel MNIST--USPS at a cost linear in the batch size, and it is more sample-efficient, achieving lower endpoint error than MMD in 13 of 15 paired runs across library sizes. By avoiding pairwise kernel evaluation, it reduces discrepancy memory by 29.8% and trains at batch sizes where kernel MMD exceeds GPU memory. These results show that PCF provides accurate and efficient invertible transport, particularly in sample- and memory-limited settings.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP
summary:
Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. The objective is to minimize the total length of all walks. In general, it is NP-hard to find any approximation for this problem in polynomial time (even if the approximation factor is allowed to depend on the number of vertices). We show that one can obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in time $n^{O(k)}$, answering an open question by Friggstad [2013].
  For the special case where all tour start vertices $s_i$ are identical and all end vertices $t_i$ are identical, we obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in polynomial time, as well as an $(O(\frac{1}ε), 1+ε)$-bicriteria approximation. For the multi-depot setting, where $s_i =t_i$ for all $i$, we obtain a constant-factor approximation in polynomial time.
  Finally, our results imply improved constant-factor approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Regret-Bounded Vehicle Routing and unit-weight Path ATSP.

title: Backbone Matters: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Networks for Semantic Segmentation of Driving Scenes on BDD100K
summary: Semantic segmentation gives an autonomous vehicle a dense, pixel-level description of its surroundings and is a core part of scene understanding. Most segmentation networks consist of an encoder (the backbone) and a decoder, yet the backbone is often chosen without a systematic comparison. This work studies this choice on the BDD100K driving dataset. Four widely used decoders (U-Net, FPN, LinkNet and PSPNet) are combined with 13 backbones from six families (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, Inception, MobileNet and EfficientNet), and all 52 models are trained with one common protocol. The best model, an FPN decoder with an EfficientNet-B4 backbone, reaches 62.6% mean intersection over union (mIoU), 89.8% accuracy and a loss of 0.092. Only two of the 52 models, both FPN with EfficientNet, exceed the 56.9% mIoU reported with the BDD100K benchmark. The effect of the backbone depends strongly on the decoder: the same EfficientNet-B4 gives 42.6% mIoU with PSPNet but 62.6% with FPN, and the gap between the best and the worst backbone ranges from 12.0 points (U-Net) to 42.5 points (FPN). The results and the scope of this study are discussed.

title: A version of the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition for full/quad pol synthetic aperture radar data
summary: Based on the Cloude/van Zyl decomposition of reflection symmetric polarimetric SAR data we present a version for full/quad polarisation data. We demonstrate both versions on X-band F-SAR data over Vejers, Denmark. Differences between the original and our version of the decomposition occur especially for very bright man-made targets. These differences come with lower entropy for our version giving an improved focus on a more pronounced dominant scattering mechanism for these objects. Interpretation of the scattering mechanism related to the full/quad pol version of the decomposition is facilitated by means of the Cloude/Pottier $\barα$ angle.

title: EmbodyAgent: Post-Training Embodied VLM Agents via Distillation, SFT, and RL
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures. Code-as-policy robot-use agent post-training
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can act as closed-loop robot-use agents (RUAs) by writing and executing control code through tool interfaces. However, turning an open-weight VLM into a high-performing embodied agent requires a complete post-training stack: out-of-the-box open VLMs fail completely at interactive tool contracts, strong frontier teachers are accessible only as black-box endpoints without exposed weights or token probabilities, and supervised imitation alone plateaus under rollout distribution shift. We present EmbodyAgent, an end-to-end post-training framework with three tightly coupled pipelines: (1) a black-box data synthesis pipeline that queries a strong teacher under a forced think-then-code contract and filters trajectories by task success; (2) an SFT pipeline that distills the explanation-and-program targets into an open-weight 9B VLM with both vision and language encoders trainable; and (3) an online RL pipeline that optimizes student-generated episodes via group-relative advantage with a runtime-error-penalized outcome reward. All three pipelines share one primitive-free Python execution tool exposing only raw visual observation and seven-dimensional end-effector control, with no action decoder and no interface shift across stages. Under a strictly separated evaluation protocol on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks (disjoint state splits, greedy test-time decoding, training-only safeguards), held-out success on 100 test states rises from 0/100 (base 9B VLM) to 14/100 (after SFT) and 84/100 (after RL), while training rollout success climbs from 8.4% to 87.7% and median model calls per episode drop from 36 to 11. We further identify a self-reinforcing runtime-error mode induced by outcome-based RL on executable code, and establish a failure-category monitoring and sampling-side curation protocol that stabilizes training.

title: Learning to Think with Images Faithfully via Adaptive Data Selection
summary: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.

title: Learn, Freeze, and Transfer an Activation Function Across Architectures
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code: https://github.com/AI4Bharat/LeFT-activation-transfer, Interactive figures: https://arunprakash-a.github.io/papers/learn-freeze-transfer/
summary: Transfer learning typically reuses knowledge acquired by a source network through its learned weights. We investigate whether a learned activation function can also be transferred and remain useful in networks trained from scratch. We study this complementary form of transfer through a learn-freeze-transfer protocol, in which the activation is optimized jointly with a source network in a single training run, and is then frozen and reused in target networks trained from scratch. A pointwise activation with globally shared parameters is independent of layer dimensions and can therefore be incorporated into networks of different architectures trained from scratch. We instantiate this protocol with FAct, a five-parameter activation represented by a two-harmonic truncated Fourier series, initialized from a Fourier approximation of GELU and learned in a Vision Transformer (ViT) on ImageNet-1K. When reused in a ViT of the same architecture trained from scratch on ImageNet-1K, the frozen activation (Frozen FAct) improves top-1 accuracy by 1.46 percentage points over GELU. Across four smaller target architectures (standard ViT, Swin Transformer, linear-attention ViT, and MLP-Mixer) and four image-classification datasets, it achieves the highest mean accuracy among eleven activation functions in 15 of 16 settings under a common training configuration, with improvements of up to 1.71 percentage points over the best conventional activation. When the learning rate and weight decay are tuned separately for each activation under the same search budget, Frozen FAct still ranks first in 11 of the 16 settings, second in four, and fourth in one. These results provide empirical evidence that a learned activation function can retain its usefulness when transferred across vision architectures, independently of the weights with which it was learned.

title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
summary: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

title: The Necessity of Acceptance & Rejection in Inferential Reasoning
summary: In this paper, we argue that acceptance and rejection constitute two fundamental positions necessary for inferential reasoning. Our central thesis is that a proposition acquires an inferential role when it is considered from a position of acceptance or rejection, rather than purely understood as propositional content. We distinguish between understanding a proposition, entertaining it hypothetically, and employing it within an inference. Particular attention is given to hypothetical reasoning and suspended judgement, which appear to challenge the necessity of adopting either position. We maintain that these cases do not undermine our thesis, since inferential reasoning can involve provisional acceptance or rejection without requiring personal belief or permanent commitment. Accordingly, the necessity of these positions should be understood as inferential rather than psychological. By examining the relationship between propositional content, inferential positions, and rational commitment, we defend the view that acceptance and rejection provide the fundamental conditions under which propositions can function within reasoning. This establishes a philosophical foundation for understanding inference through opposed rational positions.

title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
summary: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 39% of public peer reviews published in Oct-Nov 2026 (78% on a subset of reviews from Nature), and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.

title: MixReact: Physics-Based Reactive Humanoid Control from Multimodal Cues via a Discrete-Continuous Mixture of Transformers
summary: Humanoid agents in everyday environments are expected to react to diverse cues as humans do, with semantically appropriate and physically executable behaviors. Existing cue-driven reaction generation methods support only a narrow range of cue modalities and are limited to purely kinematic generation, leaving the resulting reactions susceptible to physical artifacts. To this end, we present MixReact, the first unified framework for physics-based reactive humanoid control from text, audio, and video cues, integrating a Discrete--Continuous Mixture of Transformers (DisCo-MoT) for state prediction with a History-aware Action Transformer (HAT) for physical execution. DisCo-MoT couples a discrete masked-modeling branch with a continuous autoregressive diffusion branch via one-way mixture attention within a MoT architecture. Guidance from discrete context mitigates collapse into averaged behaviors in one-to-many reaction generation, while direct prediction in continuous state space bypasses the decoding bottleneck of discrete representations. HAT then maps the predicted next state and observed execution history to executable actions, enabling robust closed-loop control in physics-based simulation. Experiments across all three modalities demonstrate consistent improvements over the baselines in fidelity, diversity, and physical consistency, while ablations validate the complementary contributions of the components. Our code will be released to facilitate future research. Project page: https://binlee26.github.io/MixReact_Page/

title: Spherical Tessellation of Circular Arrays for Massive MIMO: Favourable Propagation Conditions and Spectral Design
summary: Upper-mid-band XL-MIMO can exploit line-of-sight propagation, but periodic uniform cylindrical arrays may produce grating ridges. We analyse a spherically tessellated concentric circular antenna array with non-separable facet orientations. Under fixed normalised chord spacing and ideal facet visibility, we prove that user channels become asymptotically orthogonal and matched-filter SINR approaches the single-user SNR. Simulations confirm interference decay and SINR convergence. A spectral comparison shows that facet-normal diversity prevents the full-amplitude grating ridges of the cylindrical baseline, with the inter-facet residual decaying with array size.

title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
summary: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

title: Attention Drift Regularization with Adaptive Initialization for Domain-Robust Visual Recognition
summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a pretrained source model to unlabeled target domains without source data access, yet two critical failure modes remain unaddressed. First, attention drift: source-learned attention maps shift toward spurious or background features under distribution shift, destabilizing feature representations. Second, domain-gap-agnostic initialization: applying a single fixed source model uniformly across all target domains ignores domain gap severity, causing premature overfitting to noisy pseudo-labels under large shifts. We propose DGA-CAFC to address both failures. The Counterfactual Attention-based Feature Consistency (CAFC) module enforces feature stability by minimizing the discrepancy between representations computed under learned attention and those under counterfactual-inspired normalized perturbations, thereby promoting domain-robust features independent of spurious attention shifts. The Domain-Gap Aware Source Model Selection (DGASS) module estimates domain gap severity via target prediction entropy and selects the source model variant whose confidence level best matches the estimated gap, reducing negative transfer and stabilizing pseudo-label quality. Crucially, CAFC transfers beyond SFDA: applied as a lightweight regularizer to standard domain generalization objectives without target data. Extensive experiments across SFDA and DG benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves over recent baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of the proposed framework. Project page is available at https://visdomlab.github.io/DGA_CAFC

title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
summary: Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing remains challenging because experimental datasets are limited and process-property relationships vary across materials and operating conditions. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) govern process stability and defect formation. Conventional ML models typically use dimensional process parameters, which represent laser-material interactions only implicitly and may limit cross-material transfer. This study evaluates whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, combining laser processing conditions with material thermophysical properties, improve melt pool prediction over raw process parameters. We systematically benchmark seven models: four classical ML methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2). Experiments span 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets, covering regression of melt pool width and depth and classification of melting modes. Dimensionless features yield comparable or superior predictive performance in most settings, with the largest gains in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). Tabular foundation models generally achieve stronger classification performance than classical baselines, particularly for multi-material datasets. These findings indicate that combining physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular models can improve data-efficient melt pool modeling and support more transferable process-window identification in LPBF.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
comment: A two-stage pipeline that teaches VLAs to stop prohibited tasks safely while preserving permitted skills
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

title: FastRoverVLA: Fast Vision-Language-Action Execution for Off-Road Autonomous Driving
summary: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.

title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations
comment: this is a draft for a chapter in a forthcoming handbook on Comtemporary Modal Logic
summary: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.

title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
comment: https://twinlab-bench.github.io/ contains tasks and code. 33 pages, 6 figures, 14 tables. LLM-agent benchmark for autonomous experimental design in digital twins of real labs (physics, chemistry, wet-lab biology, materials, engineering). 13 agents evaluated: Claude Fable 5.2 45.0, Opus 5.5 40.2, GPT-6.1-sol 31.7, plus DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and others
summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

title: Beyond Covers and Titles: Evidence-First Ranking for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
summary: Short-video platforms rank new uploads before anyone has watched them, using content towers that read a video's cover, title and frames. Existing attacks on content-aware recommenders perturb pixels or features and ignore platform re-encoding, and existing defenses train against norm-bounded perturbations that neither match real edits nor preserve recommendation quality. We show with REAP, a realizable attack through {a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping and JPEG)}, that packaging edits raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points in unrelated audiences. We then observe that cold-start ranking does not need the packaging at all: a tower that sees only the video body ranks cold items best. Building on this, we propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their body, admits packaging only through a support-gated residual bounded by $γ$, and merges cold and warm rankings by rank percentile, yielding an exact certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts the attack gain by 81% and raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, while keeping the merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.

title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design
summary: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs $1.7\times$ faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.

title: STAGE: Spatio-Temporal Augmented Graph Expansion for Weakly Supervised Cross-Tweet Event Causality Discovery
summary: Causal relations in disaster-related social media of- ten span independent posts, making cross-tweet causal discovery difficult to supervise and model at scale. We propose STAGE, a framework that separates scalable cross-tweet weak-supervision construction from spatio-temporal relational learning over event occurrences. Starting from local causal seeds, STAGE retrieves semantically related event occurrences across tweets and uses a causal scorer to construct weakly labeled cross-tweet pairs. These pairs supervise a multi-head Graph Attention Network over semantically enriched event representations and a spatio- temporal context graph. We evaluate STAGE on California Wildfire and Hurricane Harvey using human-gold cross-tweet test sets and 15 baselines. Compared with local-only supervision, the constructed cross-tweet supervision improves STAGE AUPRC by 0.340 on Wildfire and 0.107 on Hurricane. STAGE achieves in-domain AUROC of 0.885 on Wildfire and 0.710 on Hurricane. Cross-disaster experiments reveal asymmetric transfer, highlighting sensitivity to dataset-specific spatio-temporal shifts. These results demonstrate the value of scalable cross-tweet supervision combined with relational event modeling for causal learning across fragmented disaster reports.

title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at ICSE 2027. Code and data: https://github.com/TankTechnology/SkillBridge
summary: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.

title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
summary: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.

title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
summary: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.

title: Cooling Noisy Population Protocols -- Vanishing-Gain Averaging and Localisation under Persistent Errors
summary: We study noise-tolerant coordination in anonymous population protocols whose agents interact in uniformly random pairs, maintain real-valued labels, and have no global clock. Each agent cools its updates using a gain $γ_k=(k+1)^{-p}$ computed from its own local interaction counter. First, for pairwise averaging with independent communication errors drawn from a fixed centred finite-variance distribution, we prove convergence with probability 1 to a common finite random value for every $1/2<p\le1$, and derive convergence-rate exponents under the same assumptions. Second, for one-dimensional localisation with fixed non-degenerate Gaussian displacement errors, we show that the one-sided RightAlign rule rectifies centred noise and cannot stabilise; a signed update based on the relative-position discrepancy restores convergence to the true agents locations up to one finite random translation. Third, we analyse the setting in which both communication errors and displacement-measurement errors depend on the physical distance between the interacting devices. For additive independent Gaussian errors, the two sources combine into one centred effective error whose variance is the sum of the distance-dependent component variances. The signed updates protocol remains convergent for every fixed finite geometry, and the average combined variance determines the leading common-translation fluctuation. These results distinguish cooling-compatible signed corrections from one-sided updates that turn persistent noise into drift.

title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
summary: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

title: Tracking Objects Through Assembly and Decomposition
summary: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.

title: Deterministic Parameterized Inapproximability of the Shortest Vector and Minimum Distance Problems
summary: The Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) and the Minimum Distance Problem (MDP) are central computational problems on lattices and linear codes, respectively. For every computable real $p\ge1$ and any constant factor, we prove that the parameterized SVP in the $\ell_p$ norm, with the distance threshold as the parameter, is W[1]-hard to approximate within factor $γ$ under deterministic reductions. The same method shows that, for every finite field, the parameterized MDP is W[1]-hard to approximate within any constant factor under deterministic reductions.

title: dLoop: Looped Diffusion Language Models via Recurrent Latent Refinement
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.

title: I See You: Initial Multi-Robot LiDAR Registration with Mutual-Observation Checks
comment: Accepted final version. IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR), Incheon, South Korea, November 2026. Project page: https://tu-darmstadt-ros-pkg.github.io/i-see-you-registration
summary: Compared to single-robot deployments, multi-robot teams can significantly improve search-and-rescue (SAR) mission success by covering large areas in parallel. To collaborate effectively, these robots must be registered in a common reference frame. Standard registration methods typically rely on external infrastructure or significant map overlap, but real deployments require infrastructure-free, stationary initial alignment for immediate operation. While global LiDAR point cloud registration addresses this, existing single-scan methods often fail silently in aliased or degenerate environments. Approaches scaling beyond two agents also remain rarely evaluated in real-world scenarios. We propose a centralized, deployment-ready framework for pre-mission multi-robot registration. Our system performs pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment and actively rejects impossible pose hypotheses via deterministic plausibility checks. We validate the framework on a real-world custom dataset of four synchronized robots in various environments with ground truth. The checks reject more than a third of the incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting less than 1% of the correct ones, and reduce the number of team registrations with a wrong robot pose by 38%. Dataset and code are publicly available.

title: What If Chain-of-Thought Is Not Enough?
summary: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.

title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
summary: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

title: LocoMuJoCo: A Comprehensive Imitation Learning Benchmark for Whole-Body Control
summary: LocoMuJoCo is an open-source benchmark for imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) on whole-body control. The library couples MuJoCo (CPU) with MJX and the MjWarp backend (GPU) under a single API, exposes 9 humanoid, 3 (musculo-)skeletal, and 4 quadruped embodiments, and ships a curated native motion-capture dataset for every humanoid, to which it can also retarget AMASS and LAFAN1. A modular plug-in architecture makes observations, rewards, control modes, terrains, and domain randomization fully interchangeable, while compact JAX implementations of many RL and IL algorithms provide JIT-compiled end-to-end training, and the companion loco-mujoco-real repository provides sim-to-real deployment. We describe the design, the SMPL-to-robot and robot-to-robot retargeting pipeline, and a usage example. LocoMuJoCo is released under MIT at https://github.com/robfiras/loco-mujoco.

title: BADAS-3.0: Real-Time Driving Perception and Planning from One Camera
summary: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.

title: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space
summary: AI agents are commonly specialized for new tasks and domains using skills, i.e. natural language instructions placed in their context. However, the discrete nature of textual skills prevents continuous optimization. Gradient-based approaches such as finetuning, on the other hand, are typically model-specific, preventing skill transfer across different agents. Since many agents today are built on vision-language models (VLMs), we can address these limitations by introducing Skill.png: a method for obtaining skill-like image inputs whose pixels are optimized with gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen VLM. Image skills are compatible with any VLM, and a single image can be optimized jointly for an ensemble of models. We show that Skill.png significantly outperforms state-of-the-art textual skills optimized using frontier LLMs in 9 of 16 settings (across 4 VLMs and 4 benchmarks) while requiring only 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens at inference time. Hybrid skills, i.e. text and image skills jointly optimized, further improve agent performance. Moreover, an image optimized with an ensemble of VLMs can successfully transfer across the models in the ensemble. Skill.png thus presents the first agent skill that can be optimized with gradient descent while retaining transfer benefits of text skills. Our code is available at: https://github.com/omseeth/skill.png

title: Exact guarantees and faster algorithms for $k$-rollercoasters
summary:
For $k\ge3$, a $k$-rollercoaster is a sequence of distinct values whose maximal increasing and decreasing runs all have length at least $k$. We discover the maximum guaranteed length $f_k(n)$ of $k$-rollercoasters appearing as subsequences of $n$-point permutations. In particular, letting $q=k-1$, we prove that $f_k(n)= \lceil n/q\rceil$ for $n\ge2q^2$, $f_k(n)= 2q-\lfloor \sqrt{2q^2-n}\rfloor$ for $q^2<n<2q^2$ and $f_k(n)= 0$ otherwise. We prove that the guarantees are tight by constructing an $n$-point permutation whose longest $k$-rollercoaster has exactly $f_k(n)$ points. Our proof extends Seidenberg's argument [Journal of the London Mathematical Society, 1959] for proving the Erdős--Szekeres theorem by representing points in a subsequence with respect to the lengths of longest monotonic (increasing and decreasing) subsequences that reach each point.
  The combinatorial proof yields a deterministic comparison-based algorithm that finds a rollercoaster of length at least $f_k(n)$ in $O(n\log f_k(n))$ time and $O(n)$ space for $n>q^2$. Independently, we give an $O(nk\log k)$-time, $O(nk)$-space algorithm for a longest $k$-rollercoaster, improving the previous $O(nk^2)$ bound. We use the dynamic program of Gawrychowski et al. [STACS 2019, Algorithmica 2022], and process its weighted predecessor queries through monotone subsequences with finger-search trees. Both algorithms return such subsequences.

title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

title: Exposure-Aware Informative Path Planning Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: This paper addresses the finite-budget exposure-aware informative path planning (IPP) problem for a fleet of mobile sensing agents. The agents map an unknown scalar field while limiting exposure to high field intensity. Existing IPP methods optimize informativeness under motion or resource constraints, but do not address field exposure constraints. We formulate exposure-aware IPP (EA-IPP) as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state Markov decision process that trades the normalized Gaussian-process (GP) information gain against a normalized measurement-derived fleet exposure index. A parameter-shared proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic is trained offline and evaluated on unseen fields. Across the radar, plume, and wildfire field families, the EA-IPP agent achieves the lowest GP reconstruction RMSE among the evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within $10\%$ of the non-learning information baseline. The minimum field exposure is approximately $34.6\%$, $20.1\%$, and $27\%$ below the non-exposure-aware baseline for radar, plume, and wildfire, respectively.

title: Scalable fault vulnerability analysis for ReRAM-based process-in-memory CNN accelerators
summary: Resistive random-access memory (ReRAM)-based processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators offer a highly efficient platform for parallel matrix-vector multiplications (VMM) in neural networks, leveraging analog computation, high density, low leakage, and non-volatility. However, their susceptibility to permanent faults, such as stuck-at-high (\textit{SaH}) and stuck-at-low (\textit{SaL}) resistance states, permanently corrupts the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) weights mapped onto ReRAM cell conductance values, thereby degrading inference accuracy and leading to system unreliability in safety-critical applications. Fault injection is a commonly used technique to assess the vulnerability of neural networks by systematically injecting faults into individual parameters and measuring the resulting accuracy degradation. Although this method is accurate, it is prohibitively time-consuming and computationally expensive, especially for large-scale CNNs. In this paper, we propose a fast, scalable, and analytical framework to quantify the fault vulnerability of convolutional neural networks deployed on ReRAM-based PIM accelerators. This method quantifies vulnerability at different granularities, including weights, kernels, and layers, without the need for exhaustive simulation, enabling the design of fault-tolerant accelerators for edge and safety-critical applications. The comparison between the results of the proposed vulnerability score (VS) metrics with performance metric of CNNs captured with fault injection simulations confirms the effectiveness of our proposed method. Unlike exhaustive fault injection, which requires days or weeks, whereas the proposed approach achieves a speedup of about $10^4\times-10^5\times$, enabling fast and accurate vulnerability analysis for large-scale CNNs within only a few minutes or hours.

title: Client Exits - A Way to Increase LLM Transparency on the Client Side
summary: Textual recommendations generated by large language models (LLMs) can be difficult to inspect. This paper introduces \emph{Client Exits}, a lightweight mechanism for enriching LLM responses while separating semantic intent from client-specific presentation. The model inserts predefined, machine-interpretable markers into its output, and the receiving client decides whether and how to realize the corresponding enrichments. This allows supplementary information to be presented as graphics, text, speech, or other modalities without prescribing a concrete interface. We implement a prototype combining a finetuned Qwen model with a modified LibreChat client. Using the Question--Option--Criteria (QOC) approach including three XML-based client exits. We evaluate two QOC-oriented model variants trained on essentially the same examples, with client-exit annotations added for one variant. Across 100 test questions, the client-exit model includes all three markers in every response. An LLM judge, informed about the mechanism without being instructed to favor it, prefers this model's answers in 66\% of the comparisons. These results demonstrate successful marker generation on the evaluated test set and support the feasibility of client-controlled enrichment.

title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.

title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
summary: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

title: Actor-Predictor Architecture for Reinforcement Learning with Formal Specification Objectives
summary: One fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) is enforcing temporal safety constraints, such as satisfying formal specifications. Existing methods often transform logic formulas into automata for state augmentation and reward shaping. However, this approach assumes that automaton construction is both feasible and tractable, which limits its applicability to small specifications and linear temporal logic (LTL). This paper proposes Actor-Predictor, a framework that learns a surrogate representation of logic progress without explicitly constructing an automaton. The predictor continuously estimates whether a partial trajectory will satisfy the formal specification in a later step, and its learned features are provided as auxiliary inputs to the actor, which is then optimized using GRPO and RWR. We show theoretically that, under sufficient predictive accuracy, the learned representation is equivalent to the automaton state. Experiments on grid world and robotic tasks in Isaac Lab demonstrate that Actor-Predictor outperforms automaton-based baselines on LTL-constrained tasks. It also performs well on non-regular formal specifications, such as $(a^n b^n)$, for which finite-automaton-based approaches are not applicable.

title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
summary: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

title: Language-Oriented Semantic Modeling for Target Language Extraction
summary: Target Language Extraction (TLE) aims to isolate speech in a target language from multilingual mixtures. Existing approaches primarily rely on acoustic modeling with language identity labels, which provide only coarse categorical guidance. In this work, we propose a language-oriented semantic modeling framework that augments acoustic extraction with language-specific semantic representations. A pre-trained speech semantic model is adapted via language-aware prompt conditioning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to generate target-language-focused semantic representations from the mixture. {These capture high-level semantic structure of the acoustics and they} are integrated into the extraction model to provide structured semantic guidance beyond identity labels. Experiments on the CommonVoiceMix dataset show that incorporating semantic representations consistently improves over acoustic-only baselines, achieving up to 1.16 dB SI-SDR gain.

title: ResVision: Spectrum-Matched Resizing and Context-Preserving Inspection for Visual Reasoning
summary: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.

title: A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics
summary: Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.

title: FirstCross: Convex Single-Photon 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views
summary: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.

title: Signed QoI Gaps for Goal-Oriented Error Estimation: Reliability and Sharpness from the Same First-Order System Residuals
summary: There are two common ways to estimate the error in a quantity of interest (QoI). The product of primal and adjoint error estimators gives a reliable but pessimistic bound. The dual-weighted residual method gives a sharp signed estimate from a more accurate approximation of the adjoint solution. We write the primal and adjoint problems as first-order systems and obtain both a reliable bound and a sharp estimate from the same residuals. The first paper of this series (arXiv:2607.23850) uses two consistent evaluators of a quantity of interest, one built from the potentials and one in which the gradients are expressed through the fluxes. We show that they differ exactly by the $A^{-1}$ inner product of the primal and adjoint constitutive residuals, and we call this difference the signed QoI gap. The identity holds for arbitrary primal and adjoint approximations. In our numerical experiments, the signed QoI gap is of the size of the larger of the errors of the two evaluators, while the product of the estimators exceeds this error by factors of up to several hundred. We therefore use the least-squares estimators to refine the mesh and the signed QoI gap to decide when to stop. We also introduce a third evaluator, built from the fluxes alone, which restores the reaction term. The resulting reaction-restored QoI gap estimates the error when reaction dominates. With the non-intrusive least-squares flux recovery, we can apply the method to any discretization that produces a conforming potential, including finite difference and finite volume schemes.

title: Predicting Surface Displacement Fields of Laser Powder Bed Fusion Parts Using STL-Derived Graphs and Part-Level Descriptors
summary: Predicting part distortion before fabrication remains challenging in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), while thermomechanical simulation is computationally expensive for repeated design evaluations. This study presents a two-branch graph attention network (GAT) to predict three-dimensional surface displacement directly from STL-derived graphs. The first branch learns geometric relationships among connected vertices of a densified STL surface mesh, while the second incorporates 12 part-level descriptors of mass distribution, build-plate contact, overhang, size, and shape. Displacement labels from ANSYS Additive Print simulations are mapped onto STL vertices using Gaussian-kernel weighted averaging. Evaluated on 117 parts using five-fold cross-validation split by part, the model achieves an R^2 of 0.946 and a mean absolute error of 0.0178 mm for displacement magnitude. Relative to a node-wise multilayer perceptron, GAT improves R^2 from 0.913 to 0.946; for build-direction displacement, R^2 increases from 0.903 to 0.939. GAT also outperforms GraphSAGE (R^2 = 0.936) and a graph convolutional network (R^2 = 0.934) across all five folds. Ablation experiments show that removing mass-distribution descriptors reduces magnitude R^2 to 0.900, while removing build-plate contact and overhang descriptors reduces it to 0.920. These results demonstrate the value of combining local mesh connectivity with global geometric descriptors to predict LPBF distortion, enabling faster design iteration and earlier identification of distortion-prone geometries.

title: Rigel-Ladon: An Option-Count Law for a One-Pass Decision Encoder, Tested on Held-Out Option Counts and Held-Out Schemas
summary: Laya is a small neural network that reads a text, a question and K written options, and returns one probability per option in a single pass. We ask how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether that can be predicted. We score nested option sets (every K-option question contains the smaller ones) on four question pools, for the released model (Base) and our fine-tune (FT), and score every item against each single rival. FT trained on one 12-option topic question (in-family); a 12-option HR (department-routing) question is out-of-family. Logit accuracy (the log of correct over incorrect answers) is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88. Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 (a log-linear rule: 1.6 and 6.7). Taking the slope from the topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy on HR predicts its other K within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base). On a 35-label pool of five schemas the law fails (5 to 11 points). Independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected: the gold-versus-rival log-odds shifts by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per doubling of K, yet pairwise answers reproduce K-way accuracy within 4.7 points. Order averaging (averaging over several orderings of the options), shortlists, a temperature law and calibrated prediction sets did not transfer (FT's 90% sets cover 84% on HR). 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held. Caveats: one model family and LLM-labelled synthetic text.

title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
summary: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.

title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
summary: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels.
